thread.title: Hillel's political decision is a self-inflicted wound and a loss for UMich
thread.title_full: Hillel's political decision is a self-inflicted wound and a loss for UMich

author: JASON PESICK
title: Hillel's political decision is a self-inflicted wound and a loss for UMich
text:
One of the jewels of the University of Michigan’s campus has long been Michigan Hillel . When I was a student in the 2000s and then again in the early 2010s, Friday night Shabbat dinners brought both Jewish and non-Jewish students together, regardless of politics. I invited my friends, including non-Jewish campus leaders, to events and discussions Hillel hosted. Hillel showcased a pluralistic Jewish community to our diverse campus.
Unfortunately, for reasons that have not yet been publicly explained in a credible way, Michigan Hillel has made a political decision to exclude student groups that do not adhere to a right-wing interpretation of Zionism. This change will isolate Hillel and Jewish students on campus. It is also a tremendous loss for the University because it weakens one of the great institutions on campus and will reduce its impact.
As The Michigan Daily reported on Sept. 9, Michigan Hillel forced the liberal but mainstream Zionist group, the University of Michigan’s J Street chapter, to disaffiliate. Cindy Hughey, Hillel’s interim executive director, stated in an email to The Daily that Hillel did not want to affiliate with advocacy groups.
Up must be down these days on Hill Street. Hillel has remained affiliated with Wolverine for Israel, whose page on Hillel’s website describes it as “the pro-Israel community supporting Zionists … at the University of Michigan” that “aim(s) to educate, support, empower, and strengthen Zionists on campus.”
Wolverine for Israel has close ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which is highly engaged in U.S. politics. In other words, what Hughey meant is that Hillel only wants to be affiliated with advocacy groups that adhere to an approved strain of Zionism. Rather than eschewing advocacy, Hillel is advocating for a specific point of view at the expense of dialogue and inclusion.
Hillel is turning inward at a time when it could better serve Jewish students by figuring out how to appeal to and make inroads on campus. Its impact will be reduced because, as enlightened leaders know, censorship is no way to win an argument or have an impact, especially on a university campus. Hillel’s ability to engage in constructive dialogue on campus will be diminished.
I am too far removed from student life to know exactly what happened, but as a University alum and longtime Hillel donor, I believe the campus community deserves answers to the following questions: Was this decision donor-driven? Was this decision made by the interim director? Was this decision, or whatever pressure led to it, a reason why there’s an interim director and the previous director left? What is the board’s position and involvement in this decision?
One of the saddest ironies is that this decision became public only days after Michael Brooks, the legendary former Michigan Hillel executive director, died on Aug. 31. During his more than 30 years as director until his retirement in 2011, he made it his mission for Hillel to welcome diverse perspectives, including on Israel. He understood this campus and knew that censoring criticism of Israel, including from liberal Zionists, would backfire and weaken Hillel’s standing on Michigan’s diverse campus.
This decision betrays his legacy, thousands of Jewish Wolverines and the values of this great public university.
LSA and Law School alum Jason Pesick is a former Editor in Chief and Editorial Page Editor of The Michigan Daily.
